The provided text exhibits a strong reliance on end-rhyme and internal sonic repetition to create a cohesive auditory structure. The passage is built around a consistent /eɪn/ rhyme scheme, evident in the pairing of "rain" and "refrain." This rhyme anchors the stanza, creating a predictable and musical cadence.

Phonologically, the text makes extensive use of alliteration and consonance. The initial /d/ sound is repeated in "dreary," "droplets," and "descended," establishing a soft, dripping auditory motif that mirrors the semantic content of rain. Similarly, the /t/ sound appears frequently in "tapping," "nature’s," and "refrain" (as part of the final consonant cluster), contributing to a staccato rhythm that mimics the "tapping out" described in the text.

Vowel sounds also play a significant role. The long /iː/ sound in "dreary," "heath" (though technically /iː/ in some dialects, often /ɛ/ in others, but here likely intended to rhyme with the softness of the scene), and "morose" creates a somber, elongated tone. The short /ɒ/ or /ɑː/ in "November" and "morose" adds weight to the description of the season.

The phrase "nature’s morose refrain" employs sibilance through the /n/ and /r/ sounds, which, combined with the /f/ in "refrain," creates a hushed, whispering quality appropriate for a "dreary night."

Regarding the question embedded in the text: The day that comes after Monday is Tuesday.
